title: Gravity drip rates in drops per minute (drop factor 20, 15 or 60)
blurb: Calculate a gravity drip rate in drops per minute using the drop factor given, with time in minutes.
question: Prescription: 5% glucose, 500 mL, IV, over 4 hours. The giving set delivers 20 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at?

teach.h: Drops, not mL; minutes, not hours
teach.body: Formal rule: drops per minute = volume (mL) × drop factor (drops/mL) ÷ time (minutes). Plain English: turn the volume into drops, turn the time into minutes, then share the drops across the minutes. The drop factor is printed on the giving set packet and is always given in the question. Drip rates are a stretch item: none appeared on the practice papers, but they are standard UK numeracy.

head: Giving set
Conventional drop factor
Typical use
teach.caption: Values vary by manufacturer. Use the drop factor printed in the question, not one from memory.

teach.h: Worked example: Mr Doyle on a community hospital ward
teach.body: Patrick Doyle, 81, needs 5% glucose 500 mL over 4 hours by gravity, giving set 20 drops/mL. Minutes = 4 × 60 = 240. Drops = 500 × 20 = 10,000. 10,000 ÷ 240 = 41.67, so 42 drops per minute. Sense-check: the pump rate would be 125 mL per hour, and at 20 drops/mL that is 2500 drops an hour, about 42 a minute.

teach.h: Same bag, different sets: 500 mL over 4 hours
teach.caption: Using the wrong drop factor changes the rate by a quarter, or threefold.

teach.text: Forgetting to change hours to minutes, or using the wrong drop factor. 500 × 20 ÷ 4 = 2500 is drops per HOUR. And a blood set (15) and a standard set (20) are not interchangeable: read the drop factor in the stem every time.

teach.body: With a 60 drops/mL burette set, drops per minute equals mL per hour, because the × 60 and the ÷ 60 cancel. A child on 45 mL per hour through a burette runs at 45 drops per minute. Round drip rates to the nearest whole number: you cannot count part of a drop.

items: Drops per minute = mL × drop factor ÷ minutes.
Change hours to minutes (× 60) before dividing.
Use the drop factor in the stem: 20, 15 and 60 give different answers.
With 60 drops/mL, drops per minute = mL per hour.
Round to the nearest whole drop at the end.

summary: You can now calculate gravity drip rates in drops per minute for standard, blood and burette giving sets, using the drop factor given. You can also catch the classic errors of leaving time in hours or using the wrong drop factor.

A.q: Prescription: 5% glucose, 500 mL, IV, over 4 hours. The giving set delivers 20 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
A.why: 500 × 20 = 10,000 drops. 4 hours = 240 minutes. 10,000 ÷ 240 = 41.67, so 42 drops per minute.

whyNot.0: This uses a drop factor of 15, not the 20 in the stem.
whyNot.1: This is the pump rate in mL per hour, not drops per minute.
whyNot.3: This leaves the time in hours, giving drops per hour.

A.q: A man is prescribed 1 unit of red cells, volume 280 mL, IV over 2 hours, through a blood giving set that delivers 15 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at?
A.why: 280 × 15 = 4200 drops. 2 hours = 120 minutes. 4200 ÷ 120 = 35 drops per minute.

whyNot.1: This uses a drop factor of 20; the blood set in the stem is 15.
whyNot.2: This is the pump rate in mL per hour.
whyNot.3: This leaves the time in hours, giving drops per hour.

A.q: A child is prescribed 0.9% sodium chloride 150 mL, IV over 5 hours, through a burette giving set that delivers 60 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at?
A.why: 150 × 60 = 9000 drops. 5 hours = 300 minutes. 9000 ÷ 300 = 30 drops per minute (the same as 30 mL per hour).

whyNot.0: This uses a drop factor of 20, not the 60 in the stem.
whyNot.1: This leaves the time in hours, giving drops per hour.
whyNot.2: This leaves out the drop factor and gives mL per minute.

B.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 1000 mL, IV, over 12 hours. The giving set delivers 20 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
B.why: 1000 × 20 = 20,000 drops. 12 hours = 720 minutes. 20,000 ÷ 720 = 27.78, so 28 drops per minute.

whyNot.0: This cuts off the decimals instead of rounding 27.78 up.
whyNot.2: This uses a drop factor of 15, not the 20 in the stem.
whyNot.3: This is the pump rate in mL per hour.

B.q: Prescription: an antibiotic in 0.9% sodium chloride, 100 mL, IV, over 40 minutes. The giving set delivers 20 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at?

whyNot.0: This is the pump rate in mL per hour, not drops per minute.
whyNot.1: This uses a drop factor of 15, not the 20 in the stem.
whyNot.2: This treats 40 minutes as a full hour.

B.q: A child is prescribed 0.9% sodium chloride 360 mL, IV over 12 hours, through a burette giving set that delivers 60 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at?
B.why: 360 × 60 = 21,600 drops. 12 hours = 720 minutes. 21,600 ÷ 720 = 30 drops per minute.

whyNot.1: This uses a drop factor of 20, not the 60 in the stem.
whyNot.2: This leaves the time in hours, giving drops per hour.
whyNot.3: This uses a drop factor of 15, not the 60 in the stem.

C.q: A 1000 mL bag of 0.9% sodium chloride has 600 mL left. The remaining fluid is to run over 5 hours through a giving set that delivers 20 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at?
C.why: 600 × 20 = 12,000 drops. 5 hours = 300 minutes. 12,000 ÷ 300 = 40 drops per minute.

whyNot.0: This uses the full 1000 mL, not the 600 mL remaining.
whyNot.1: This is the pump rate in mL per hour.
whyNot.3: This uses a drop factor of 15, not the 20 in the stem.

C.q: A 500 mL bag is running by gravity at 25 drops per minute through a giving set that delivers 20 drops/mL. How many minutes will the bag take to finish?
C.why: Total drops = 500 × 20 = 10,000. 10,000 ÷ 25 drops per minute = 400 minutes.

whyNot.0: This leaves out the drop factor.
whyNot.2: This uses a drop factor of 15, not 20.
whyNot.3: This gives the time in hours (6.67) but labels it minutes.

C.q: A woman is prescribed 1 unit of red cells, volume 300 mL, IV over 2 hours, through a blood giving set that delivers 15 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
C.why: 300 × 15 = 4500 drops. 2 hours = 120 minutes. 4500 ÷ 120 = 37.5, which rounds up to 38 drops per minute.

whyNot.1: This rounds 37.5 down; a 5 rounds up.
whyNot.2: This uses a drop factor of 20; the blood set in the stem is 15.
whyNot.3: This is the pump rate in mL per hour.

reteach.title: Drops ÷ minutes
reteach.question: 120 mL is to run over 1 hour with a 20 drops/mL set. How many drops per minute?

blocks.body: 120 mL × 20 = 2400 drops. 1 hour = 60 minutes. 2400 ÷ 60 = 40 drops per minute.

blocks.text: Stopping at 2400: that is the number of drops in the whole hour, not per minute.

explain.body: Drops per minute = mL × drop factor ÷ minutes.

test.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 120 mL, IV, over 1 hour. The giving set delivers 20 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at?

whyNot.1: This is the pump rate in mL per hour.
whyNot.3: This uses a drop factor of 15, not the 20 in the stem.

test.q: Prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride, 1000 mL, IV, over 6 hours. The giving set delivers 20 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
test.why: 1000 × 20 = 20,000 drops. 6 hours = 360 minutes. 20,000 ÷ 360 = 55.56, so 56 drops per minute.

whyNot.0: This leaves the time in hours, giving drops per hour.
whyNot.1: This uses a drop factor of 15, not the 20 in the stem.
whyNot.3: This is the pump rate in mL per hour.

test.q: A child is receiving fluid at 45 mL per hour through a burette giving set that delivers 60 drops/mL. How many drops per minute is this?
test.why: 45 mL × 60 drops/mL = 2700 drops per hour. 2700 ÷ 60 = 45 drops per minute.

whyNot.0: This uses a drop factor of 20, not the 60 in the stem.
whyNot.1: This is drops per hour, not per minute.
whyNot.2: This leaves out the drop factor and gives mL per minute.

explain.body: A blood giving set in these questions delivers 15 drops/mL. Use 15, not 20, when the stem says so.

test.q: A man is prescribed 1 unit of red cells, volume 250 mL, IV over 2 hours, through a blood giving set that delivers 15 drops/mL. How many drops per minute should the infusion run at? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
test.why: 250 × 15 = 3750 drops. 2 hours = 120 minutes. 3750 ÷ 120 = 31.25, so 31 drops per minute.

whyNot.0: This uses a drop factor of 20; the blood set in the stem is 15.
whyNot.2: This rounds 31.25 up; the first decimal is 2.
whyNot.3: This is the pump rate in mL per hour.
